title: Topic Drill: Reading Informational Texts (Set B)

items.stem:
The Alder Ridge Volunteer Fire Station will hold its first open house on Saturday, from ten until two. Visitors can climb aboard the two engines, try on a child-sized helmet, and learn how to check a smoke alarm battery. Firefighters will also demonstrate how crews use thermal cameras to find hot spots behind walls. Parking is available behind the library, and a shuttle will run every fifteen minutes. Admission is free, though donations toward new hose will be welcome.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the news brief?
options: The station is raising money so it can buy a third engine this year
Thermal cameras are replacing smoke alarm checks in local homes
Visitors must take a shuttle because parking at the station is closed
The station is hosting a free open house with hands-on activities
items.explanation: The brief announces a free Saturday open house where visitors can board engines, try helmets and watch demonstrations. Donations toward hose are only an optional detail, not a plan for a third engine. Thermal cameras are demonstrated, not used to replace alarms, and the shuttle is a convenience from library parking, not a requirement.

items.stem:
Alder Ridge Station training schedule: Mondays are for hose drills at the tower behind the station, beginning at 6:30 p.m. Wednesdays are reserved for medical practice, led by an emergency technician who visits from the county. On the first Saturday of each month, members clean and test every piece of equipment, a job that usually lasts until noon. New recruits attend all three sessions during their first year, but may skip the Wednesday sessions once they hold a medical card.

According to the schedule, when do members clean and test the equipment?
options: On the first Saturday of each month
Every Monday beginning at 6:30 p.m.
On Wednesdays, after the medical practice ends
Once a year, when recruits earn a medical card
items.explanation: The schedule says members clean and test every piece of equipment on the first Saturday of each month, usually until noon. Monday evenings are for hose drills at the tower, not equipment checks. Wednesdays are for medical practice with a visiting technician. The medical card only lets recruits skip Wednesday sessions, and it has no link to equipment testing.

items.stem:
Lucia Ferreira joined the volunteer station at nineteen, mainly because her brother had. She kept a notebook in her coat pocket, and after every call she wrote down one thing she would do differently. Eleven years later the notebook is held together with tape, and the station’s training officer has asked to copy its pages for new recruits. Lucia says she never planned to teach anyone; she only wanted to stop making the same mistake twice.

What can be inferred about the notebook from the profile?
options: It was assigned to Lucia by the training officer as part of her duties during her first year
Its notes have proved useful enough that others want to learn from them
It records only the calls that ended badly for the station
Lucia plans to hand it over to her brother when she retires
items.explanation: The training officer wants to copy its pages for recruits, which suggests the notes are valuable to others, though Lucia only meant them for herself. The profile says she began the habit on her own, so it was not assigned. It records one lesson from every call, not only bad ones, and her brother is mentioned only as why she joined.

items.stem:
To the residents of Alder Ridge: Last winter our station answered three calls where the nearest hydrant was buried under a ridge of plowed snow, and crews lost precious minutes digging. We ask each household on a hydrant block to shovel a path three feet wide around it after every snowfall. You need do nothing more than that, because the firefighters will handle the rest. Thank you for helping us reach your neighbors faster. Sincerely, Hector Bell, Fire Chief

What is the author’s main purpose in writing the letter?
options: To report how many calls the station answered during the winter
To explain why snowplows tend to bury hydrants on side streets
To ask residents to keep hydrants clear after snow
To announce a new rule that will fine households that leave snow uncleared
items.explanation: The chief makes a direct request: shovel a three-foot path around the hydrant after each snowfall. The three calls are evidence for the request, not the point of the letter. Plows burying hydrants is mentioned only as the problem, and the letter offers thanks, not penalties, so no fine is announced.

items.stem:
The Alder Ridge pancake breakfast is the best bargain in the county, and it knows it. Stacks arrive hot and uneven, flipped by firefighters who debate batter the way other people debate sports. The coffee is weak, the syrup is generous, and the line, though long, moves with surprising cheer. I came for breakfast and stayed for an hour, laughing at a retired captain’s story about a stubborn goat on a ladder.

Which word best describes the tone of this review?
options: mildly disappointed
warmly humorous
strictly technical
anxiously urgent
items.explanation: Phrases such as ‘and it knows it,’ the batter debate and the goat story show a playful, affectionate voice, so warmly humorous fits. The weak coffee is a small joke, not a sign of disappointment. The writer gives no measurements or procedures, so the tone is not technical, and nothing in the review expresses worry or pressure.

items.stem:
Every spring the fire station’s engine bay doubles as a classroom. Third graders file in, and a firefighter in full gear kneels so the children can see that the mask and air tank do not turn him into a monster. Children who once hid from the hissing breathing apparatus end up asking to hear it again. The visit lasts forty minutes, and nobody is hurried toward the door.

As used in the passage, what does the word “file” most nearly mean?
options: store away in a cabinet
make a formal complaint
enter in a line
smooth with a rough tool
items.explanation: Here the children are entering the engine bay, so “file in” means to walk in a line, one after another. The meaning of storing papers does not fit people entering a room. A formal complaint would not describe a class visit, and smoothing with a tool is a different sense that makes no sense with third graders.

items.stem:
When a call comes in, the county dispatcher sends a tone to every member’s pager, and the pager then announces the address and the kind of emergency. Members who live within five minutes of the station drive straight there. Those who live farther away head directly to the scene once the engine has left. The first four members to reach the station staff the engine, and everyone else follows in a personal vehicle.

How is the passage mainly organized?
options: As a sequence that follows a call from dispatch to response
As a comparison of the training that near and far members receive
As a problem followed by several proposed solutions
As a list of definitions of emergency terms
items.explanation: The passage moves in time order: the dispatcher sends a tone, the pager announces the call, nearby members go to the station, and distant members go to the scene. That is a sequence. It does not compare training, pose a problem with solutions, or define vocabulary terms, although the roles of near and far members are mentioned.

items.stem:
Notice from Marlow Street Dance: Because the floorboards in Studio B are being sanded this week, all intermediate ballet classes will move to the larger Studio A. Studio A has mirrors on only one wall, so teachers will rotate each class to let every row face the glass in turn. Tap lessons are canceled until the floor is sealed, since fresh varnish cannot take the pounding of metal shoes. Regular schedules resume on Monday.

According to the notice, why are tap lessons canceled?
options: Studio A has mirrors on only one wall
Intermediate ballet needs the larger studio all week
The teachers are away while the floors are sanded
Fresh varnish cannot yet handle metal tap shoes
items.explanation: The notice states that tap lessons are canceled because fresh varnish cannot take the pounding of metal shoes. The one-wall mirrors explain why ballet classes rotate, not why tap is canceled. Ballet moving to Studio A is a separate effect of the sanding, and no teacher absence is mentioned anywhere.

items.stem:
Text 1: The Marlow Street recital is worth every ticket. Seven-year-olds in paper wings crossed the stage with total seriousness, and the older students’ jazz number had the audience clapping in time. The only flaw was the sound system, which hissed through the quiet pieces.

Text 2: I enjoyed the recital, but I wish the program had been shorter. Eighteen numbers kept the children up well past bedtime, and the hissing speakers made the slow dances hard to appreciate.

On which point do the two reviews agree?
options: The sound system was a weakness
The program ran too long
The jazz number was the highlight
The youngest dancers were not serious enough
items.explanation: Both writers mention hissing sound equipment: the first says it hissed through quiet pieces, the second says the speakers hurt the slow dances. Only the second review complains about length. Only the first praises the jazz number, and the first actually admires the youngest dancers for their total seriousness.

items.stem:
Imani Cole began at the Marlow Street studio unable to hold a turn for more than a second. She practiced in her kitchen with a dish towel on the tile, spinning until the towel stayed put. Within a year she had moved up two levels, and her teacher, Mr. Okafor, now uses her kitchen trick in class. He says she did not have the most talent, but she had the most repetition.

Which detail from the profile best shows that Imani’s progress came from practice?
options: She could not hold a turn for a second at the start
She spun in her kitchen until the towel stayed put
She moved up two levels within a year
Mr. Okafor now teaches her kitchen trick to others
items.explanation: Spinning at home until the towel stayed put is a direct example of repeated effort, so it supports the claim. Her weak start shows where she began, not how she improved. Moving up two levels is the result rather than the cause, and the teacher borrowing her trick shows its value but not her practice.

items.stem:
A sprung dance floor rests on a layer of foam blocks or flexible supports beneath the surface. When a dancer lands from a jump, the floor gives slightly and then returns, absorbing part of the force that would otherwise travel into the knees and ankles. A concrete floor does the opposite, returning almost nothing. For this reason, studios that teach leaps and turns invest in the hidden layer, even though students never see it.

What is the main idea of the article?
options: Concrete is the best surface for learning turns
Studios hide their floors because students dislike foam
Foam blocks are too costly for studios to install under most floors
A sprung floor protects dancers by absorbing the force of landings
items.explanation: The article explains that a sprung floor gives when a dancer lands, taking some force off the knees and ankles, which is why studios pay for it. Concrete is described as returning almost nothing, so it is not best. Students never seeing the layer is only a detail, and cost is never discussed.

items.stem:
Dear Ms. Varga, Thank you for the hour you spent with my daughter after Thursday’s class. When she came home she did not mention her missed steps; she showed me the combination she had finally understood. Last month she wanted to quit. I do not know what you said to her, but this morning she asked whether she could go early on Saturday and practice on the stage floor. With gratitude, Pamela Tran

What can be inferred about the daughter from the letter?
options: She still plans to quit at the end of the month
She resents having been kept after class
Her confidence has returned since the extra help
She no longer cares whether she learns the steps
items.explanation: Showing off the combination and asking to practice early on Saturday suggest her confidence has come back after the extra hour, in contrast to last month when she wanted to quit. Nothing indicates she plans to quit now, and her eagerness contradicts both resentment and indifference toward learning.

items.stem:
Spring schedule, Marlow Street Dance. Beginner tap meets Tuesdays at 4:00, directly before junior jazz at 5:00. Adult ballet is offered on Wednesday evenings at 7:00 and again on Saturday mornings at 9:30. The Saturday session is limited to eight students so that the teacher can adjust each person at the barre. Registration for either ballet session closes the Friday before the first class. Tap students must bring their own shoes, while ballet shoes may be borrowed from the front desk.

Why is the Saturday ballet session limited to eight students?
options: Because the desk has only eight pairs of shoes to lend
Because it follows beginner tap in the same room
Because registration closes before the first class
So the teacher can adjust each person at the barre
items.explanation: The schedule gives the reason directly: a limit of eight lets the teacher adjust each student at the barre. Borrowed ballet shoes are mentioned, but with no count. Beginner tap runs on Tuesdays, not before the Saturday class, and the registration deadline concerns when to sign up, not the class size.

items.stem:
Stretching cold muscles is a common mistake. A dancer who bends to the floor before warming up risks pulling a hamstring, because tight muscle fibers resist sudden lengthening. Instead, begin with five minutes of gentle movement, such as marching in place or small leg swings, to raise body temperature. Save the long holds for the end of class, when the muscles are warm and willing.

What is the author’s main purpose in this passage?
options: To advise dancers on when to stretch
To argue that dancers should never stretch at all
To describe how hamstring muscles are built
To entertain readers with a story about an injury
items.explanation: The author tells dancers to warm up first and save long stretches for the end of class, so the purpose is advice on timing. The author endorses stretching later rather than banning it. Hamstrings are mentioned only as a risk, and there is no story or narrative anywhere in the passage.

items.stem:
The first time I stood at the barre, I felt like a lamp post among swans. Everyone else’s shoulders hung loose; mine were up near my ears. Madame Kessel walked behind us tapping her cane and saying nothing, which was worse than any scolding. When she stopped at my spot, I braced for the verdict. She only lowered my shoulders with two fingers and moved on. I have been trying to deserve that small kindness ever since.

Which phrase best describes the narrator’s tone?
options: angry resentment toward a teacher who is harsh and unfair
humorous self-doubt that turns to appreciation
bored indifference toward the lesson
proud confidence about an early skill
items.explanation: The lamp post among swans image is a joke at the narrator’s own expense, and the closing line about deserving the small kindness shows gratitude. The teacher is silent, not harsh, so anger does not fit. The narrator feels nervous rather than bored, and tense shoulders show no confidence.

items.stem:
The Keller Junction Railway Museum has reopened its roundhouse after an eight-month repair of the roof. Visitors can again walk beneath a restored steam locomotive that sits above an open inspection pit, a feature the museum calls its most requested. The building also holds a small workshop where volunteers rebuild brass fittings. Admission rises by one dollar this season, a change the museum says will help cover the cost of upkeep.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the news brief?
options: The museum raised admission to pay for a new locomotive
Volunteers have stopped rebuilding brass fittings
A repaired roundhouse has reopened to museum visitors
The roof repair took far longer than the museum planned
items.explanation: The brief is chiefly about the roundhouse reopening after repair, with details about the locomotive and the workshop. The extra dollar helps cover upkeep, not a new locomotive. Volunteers still rebuild fittings in the workshop, and the length of the repair is stated as eight months with no comment on a delay.

items.stem:
The museum’s curator is meticulous about labels. Before any placard is printed, she checks each date against two sources and walks the display to be sure the text can be read from a wheelchair. Volunteers sometimes joke that she would measure a comma if she could. Visitors rarely notice her effort, which she considers the highest compliment.

As used in the passage, what does the word “meticulous” most nearly mean?
options: extremely careful about details
easily annoyed by small noises
famous for giving public speeches
relaxed about deadlines and rules
items.explanation: Checking each date against two sources and testing sightlines from a wheelchair show a person who attends closely to small details, which is the meaning of meticulous. Nothing mentions noise, speeches or deadlines, and relaxed work would contradict the volunteers’ joke that she would measure a comma.

items.stem:
Steam locomotives and diesel locomotives both pull trains, but they do it differently. A steam engine burns coal to boil water, and the expanding steam pushes pistons attached to the wheels. A diesel engine burns fuel in a motor that turns a generator, and the electricity it makes spins motors on the axles. Steam engines need frequent stops for water and coal, while diesels can run much longer between refuelings, which is one reason railroads replaced most steam engines.

How is the passage mainly organized?
options: It tells the history of one railroad in order of years
It lists the parts of a train from the front to the back
It contrasts two kinds of engines and one result
It poses a question and then argues against it
items.explanation: The passage sets steam and diesel engines side by side, explaining how each works, then ends with refueling needs and why railroads switched, which is a result of the difference. It gives no dates or railroad history, does not list train parts in order, and never asks or argues against a question.

items.stem:
Last winter, the museum’s gift shop sold out of wooden whistle toys in nine days, which surprised the staff. A short video of a child blowing one, posted by a visitor, had been shared widely that week. Within days, orders arrived from three other states. The volunteer buyer, who had ordered only forty, spent the next month on the phone with the maker, a small family workshop, to arrange a rushed second batch.

What caused the gift shop to sell out of the whistles?
options: The maker lowered the price of the whistles
A visitor’s video of a child blowing one was shared widely
The museum advertised the toys widely in three other states and online
The volunteer buyer had ordered far too few on purpose
items.explanation: The passage ties the sellout to a visitor’s video that spread that week, after which orders came in from other states. A price cut and museum advertising are never mentioned. The buyer ordered only forty, but that was a modest guess, not a deliberate attempt to run short, and the orders from other states followed the video.

items.stem:
Volunteer sign-up note: Please read before choosing your Saturday. Ticket booth shifts are quiet until noon, then busy until closing. Track-walk shifts require sturdy boots and a signed safety card, which takes two evenings to earn. Workshop shifts have no waiting list because, frankly, most people hesitate to sit near the grinder. If you are new, the front desk coordinator recommends starting at the ticket booth.

What can be inferred about the workshop shifts?
options: They require the same safety card that track walkers must earn first
They are the shortest shifts offered on Saturdays
They are reserved for experienced volunteers
They are easy to book because many volunteers avoid them
items.explanation: The note says there is no waiting list because people hesitate to sit near the grinder, so the shifts stay open since many volunteers avoid them. The safety card is tied to track-walk shifts only. No shift lengths are given, and the coordinator’s advice to start at the ticket booth does not make the workshop experienced-only.

items.stem:
Text 1: The Keller Junction timetable board is the museum’s best teaching tool. Each card lists a train that really ran, with its departure, stops and cargo, so visitors can plan an imaginary trip.

Text 2: The timetable board looks impressive, but most visitors walk past it. The cards are printed in small type, and there is no place to sit and read. If the museum enlarged the type and added a bench, I believe more people would try the imaginary trips.

How does the approach of Text 2 differ from that of Text 1?
options: It describes the cargo of the trains, while Text 1 lists only departures
It proposes improvements instead of only praising the board
It praises the board, while Text 1 criticizes its small type
It recommends adding a bench, and Text 1 recommends the same
items.explanation: Text 1 simply praises the board as a teaching tool, while Text 2 gives criticism and suggests larger type and a bench. Cargo appears in Text 1, not Text 2. Text 2 is the one that criticizes the type, and only Text 2 mentions a bench, so the claim that both recommend it is wrong.

items.stem:
Museum staff noticed that families linger longest at the signal-lever exhibit. Children pull the levers and watch lights change on a model track, and adults often join in. Staff counted visitors at the exhibit on three Saturdays and found that it never stood empty. By contrast, the display of old tickets in the next room drew only an occasional glance. The museum now plans to add a second lever panel nearby.

Which detail best supports the claim that the lever exhibit is popular?
options: Counts on three Saturdays found it never empty
Children pull the levers and watch lights change
The ticket display drew only an occasional glance
The museum plans to add a second lever panel
items.explanation: A count on three Saturdays showing the exhibit never empty is direct evidence of popularity. The description of children pulling levers explains the activity but does not measure interest. The ticket display is a contrasting exhibit, and the planned panel is a response to popularity, not proof of it.

items.stem:
A dovetail joint locks two boards together with interlocking wedges, like fingers folded between one another. Because each wedge is wider at its tip than at its base, the boards cannot be pulled apart in one direction. This is why drawers made by hand often keep their shape for generations, even after the glue has dried out. Modern drawers often use screws or staples, which work well enough but loosen over years of opening and closing.

What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Staples and screws are always stronger than any joint made by hand
Hand-built drawers cost too much for most households
Dovetail joints hold boards by their shape, not only by glue
Glue is the most important part of any drawer
items.explanation: The passage explains that wedge-shaped dovetails keep boards locked even after glue fails, so shape matters more than adhesive. Screws and staples are said to loosen with time, not to outperform handwork. Cost is never discussed, and the dried-out glue detail argues against calling glue the key part.

items.stem:
Customers often ask Rosa Delgado why her cabinet shop’s prices are higher than a warehouse store’s. She answers by pulling a drawer from each. Hers glides shut with a soft sigh; the other catches and rattles. “You are not paying for wood,” she tells them. “You are paying for the hundred small decisions nobody sees.” Most customers laugh, then reach for the checkbook.

As used in the passage, what does the word “catches” most nearly mean?
options: wins a prize
notices by surprise
becomes ill
snags partway
items.explanation: The drawer from the warehouse store is contrasted with one that glides shut, so “catches and rattles” describes a drawer that snags and sticks. Winning a prize and noticing something by surprise do not describe motion in a drawer, and becoming ill is a sense that cannot apply to furniture.

items.stem:
In March the Dunmore Cabinet Shop began storing its lumber in a heated room for two weeks before cutting. The change was suggested by the apprentice, Theo, after three doors warped on a kitchen job. Wood left in a cold, damp yard swells, then shrinks as it dries indoors, and the doors had twisted for exactly that reason. Since the change, the shop has had no warped doors, and Theo has been asked to write the new rule on the wall.

According to the passage, why did the three doors warp?
options: The wood changed size as it dried after damp, cold storage
Theo cut the boards too quickly and without letting them dry
The kitchen job used lumber that had been heated
The glue was applied before the boards were cut
items.explanation: The passage says wood stored in a cold, damp yard swells and then shrinks as it dries indoors, and that is why the doors twisted. Theo is credited with the fix, not the fault. Heated storage is the remedy, not the cause, and glue and cutting order are never mentioned.

items.stem:
Notice to customers: Starting Monday, the Dunmore Cabinet Shop will close at three o’clock on Fridays so the crew can service the saws and clean the dust collection system. Special orders must now be placed by Thursday noon to be included in the following week’s schedule. Pickups after three on Fridays can be arranged by calling ahead. We apologize for any inconvenience and thank you for your patience.

What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To persuade customers to place more special orders
To inform customers of a change in hours and order deadlines
To explain how the shop’s dust collection systems operate in detail
To apologize for a late delivery of finished cabinets
items.explanation: The notice reports an earlier Friday closing and a Thursday noon deadline for special orders, so its purpose is to inform. It does not try to sell more orders or explain machinery, since the dust system is mentioned only as the reason for closing. The apology covers the changed hours, not any late delivery.

items.stem:
The tool cabinet I ordered from Dunmore arrived two days early, and I confess I opened the crate expecting a scratch. There was none. Every drawer slid out on the first try, and the shallow one at the top fits my chisels like a hand in a glove. Is it perfect? Almost. The key is a little stiff. But I plan to leave it that way; a stiff key tells me the lock is serious.

Which phrase best describes the tone of the review?
options: sharply disappointed and demanding
neutral and uninterested in the cabinet it describes
fearful about future problems
pleasantly impressed, with a touch of humor
items.explanation: The writer praises the early arrival, the unscratched wood and the smooth drawers, and jokes that a stiff key shows a serious lock, so the tone is pleased with some humor. The one complaint is small and treated lightly, so the tone is not sharp. The writer is clearly engaged and shows no worry.

items.stem:
Shop log, Thursday. Moved the planer to the north wall so the afternoon sun does not hit the blade guard. Theo has asked three times this week why the dust collector clogs, and each time I have told him to check the filter first. Today he found the filter clean and the hose crushed under a pallet. He said nothing; he just grinned and wrote it on the checklist.

What can be inferred about Theo from the log?
options: He is careless about shop equipment
He wants the planer moved to another wall
He has learned to track down problems on his own
He will stop asking questions about the machines
items.explanation: Theo followed the advice to check the filter, then looked further and found the crushed hose, and he added it to the checklist, which shows growing skill at troubleshooting. The log does not show carelessness or any opinion about the planer’s location, and nothing says he will stop asking questions in future.

items.stem:
Sanding a tabletop takes three steps. First, use coarse paper to level the surface and remove saw marks, moving with the grain. Next, switch to medium paper to erase the scratches the coarse paper left behind. Finally, use fine paper for a smooth finish before applying any stain. Skipping a step leaves marks that stain will highlight rather than hide.

How is the passage mainly organized?
options: As types of tabletop damage grouped by cause
As steps in the order they should be done
As two opinions that are presented and then compared
As a description of a table from top to bottom
items.explanation: The signal words first, next and finally show a step-by-step order, and the closing sentence adds a consequence of skipping one. The passage does not sort damage by cause, set two opinions against each other, or describe a table’s physical parts in order from top to bottom.

items.stem:
Quarterly report, Dunmore Cabinet Shop. The shop completed eleven kitchens, four closet systems and nineteen small repairs. Kitchens took an average of five weeks from measurement to installation, one week longer than last quarter, mostly because a hinge supplier shipped late. Closet systems, which are built from stock panels, took only ten days each. Customers reported satisfaction with the work, but two asked for clearer scheduling.

According to the report, why did kitchens take longer this quarter?
options: The shop built more closet systems
Customers asked for clearer scheduling
A hinge supplier shipped late
Stock panels were hard to cut and fit
items.explanation: The report says kitchens averaged five weeks, one week longer than before, mostly because a hinge supplier shipped late. Closet systems were quicker at ten days and are not blamed for the delay. The scheduling requests came from customers after the fact, and stock panels are mentioned only for closets.

items.stem:
The Greenbelt Delivery Cooperative is owned by its drivers. Each of the twenty-two members holds one vote, no matter how many routes he or she drives, and profits are divided by the miles each member drove. The arrangement began when a regional courier firm closed its local depot and left its drivers without work. Members now set their own rates, choose their own schedules, and meet monthly to argue over both.

What is the main idea of the profile?
options: A driver-owned cooperative shares control and profits
A courier firm closed its depot and dismissed its drivers
Members argue so often that the cooperative may close soon
Drivers who cover more routes receive more votes
items.explanation: The profile describes shared ownership with one vote per member and profits divided by miles driven. The depot closing is only how the cooperative began. The monthly arguments are a detail, not a sign of closing, and the text says each member gets one vote no matter how many routes are driven.

items.stem:
The cooperative’s dispatcher, Ngozi Bell, is known for her terse messages. A typical text reads, “Dock 4. Noon. Fragile.” New drivers worry the notes are unfriendly, but veterans know better: the shortness is a sign of trust. She does not waste words explaining what she expects you to understand.

As used in the passage, what does the word “terse” most nearly mean?
options: long, detailed and full of explanations
angry and loud
carefully hidden
brief and to the point
items.explanation: The sample message is only three short phrases, and the passage says she does not waste words, so terse means brief and to the point. Long and detailed is the opposite. Nothing suggests she shouts or is angry, and her messages are sent openly, not concealed.

items.stem:
Parcels at the cooperative’s hub move through four stations. At the first, a scanner reads each label and assigns a route code. At the second, workers sort parcels into bins by code. At the third, drivers load the bins in the order of their stops, so the last stop is loaded first. At the fourth, a supervisor checks the load against the manifest before the van leaves. Any parcel without a code goes to a shelf for review.

How is the passage mainly organized?
options: The stations are ranked from most to least important
A problem is described and then a solution is argued
The stations follow the path a parcel travels
Two hubs are compared by speed and cost
items.explanation: Each station is introduced with first, second, third and fourth, following the path of a parcel, which is a sequence. The passage never ranks stations by importance, never argues a solution to a problem, and describes only one hub, so no comparison of hubs is made.

items.stem:
When fuel prices rose in spring, the Greenbelt cooperative did not raise its rates. Instead, members voted to group deliveries by neighborhood so each van made fewer trips. The change cut daily mileage by about a fifth, which more than covered the extra cost of fuel. Customers noticed only that their parcels now arrived within a two-hour window instead of at scattered times.

What was the effect of grouping deliveries by neighborhood?
options: Customers received parcels at random times of the day, as before
The cooperative raised its rates to cover fuel
Members voted to reduce their own pay
Vans drove fewer miles, which offset the higher fuel cost
items.explanation: Grouping by neighborhood cut daily mileage by about a fifth, which more than covered the extra fuel cost. Arrival times became more predictable, not random, so customers could plan for the two-hour window. The text says the cooperative did not raise rates, and nothing mentions a pay cut for members.

items.stem:
Driver’s notebook, Tuesday. The new apartment building on Pike Street has no intercom, and the front door sticks. I left four parcels on the stoop last week, and two were gone by evening. Today I rang every bell until a tenant came down to let me in. It took twelve minutes, which is why I am adding half an hour to Pike Street in my route plan from now on.

What can be inferred about the driver’s decision?
options: The driver dislikes the tenants on Pike Street
The driver values safe delivery over finishing the route quickly
The driver plans to leave parcels on the stoop again to save time
The building will soon install an intercom
items.explanation: After losing two parcels from the stoop, the driver chooses to spend extra time on Pike Street, showing that safe delivery matters more than speed. No dislike of tenants is shown, since a tenant helped. Leaving parcels outside is the practice being abandoned, and no intercom plan is mentioned.

items.stem:
Text 1: Our cooperative should adopt electric vans. They cost more to buy, but charging is cheaper than fuel, and a quieter fleet would be welcome in the neighborhoods we serve.

Text 2: Electric vans are a fine idea in theory, but our longest routes run well beyond what one charge can cover. Until the range improves, I would rather replace our oldest gas vans with newer, cleaner ones.

How do the two texts differ in what they recommend?
options: Text 1 backs electric vans, while Text 2 prefers gas vans
Text 1 opposes new vans, and Text 2 supports them
Text 1 cites range, while Text 2 cites charging costs and quiet
Both texts recommend keeping the oldest vans
items.explanation: Text 1 argues for electric vans because charging is cheaper than fuel, while Text 2 doubts their range on long routes and would replace old gas vans with newer ones. The texts do not swap positions. Range is Text 2’s point and cost is Text 1’s, and Text 2 wants the oldest vans replaced.

items.stem:
To the members: I propose we add a Sunday route. Last month, thirty-one customers asked for weekend delivery, and nine of them said they would switch to us from a rival service if we offered it. A Sunday route would need only two drivers, and volunteers have already signed up. The one drawback is wear on the vans, but we can rotate vehicles to spread it.

Which detail is the strongest evidence that customers want a Sunday route?
options: Volunteers have already signed up to drive
A Sunday route would need only two drivers on staff
The vans can be rotated to spread the wear
Thirty-one customers requested weekend delivery
items.explanation: Customer requests are the direct evidence of demand, and the nine who would switch strengthen it. Volunteer drivers show the route is feasible, not wanted. The two-driver need describes cost and staffing, and the van rotation responds to a drawback rather than showing that customers want the service.

items.stem:
The Hartwell College bookstore will begin renting textbooks next semester, a change expected to lower costs for students in large lecture courses. Rented books must be returned by the last day of exams, and pencil highlighting is allowed, but pen is not. Students who prefer to buy may still do so, and the store will continue its buyback days. A table near the entrance will list the titles that can be rented.

What is the main idea of the news brief?
options: The bookstore will offer textbook rentals alongside buying
Students may no longer highlight in any textbook
The bookstore will end its buyback days after this semester
Large lecture courses will drop their required books
items.explanation: The brief announces that rentals will start while buying remains an option. Highlighting is permitted in pencil, so students are not banned from it. The store says buyback days will continue, and nothing suggests that any course will stop requiring textbooks or that the store plans to remove them from its shelves.

items.stem:
To the Editor: The campus bookstore’s new rule that backpacks must be left at the door is unfair to commuters. Many of us carry laptops and lunches, and the lockers by the entrance are always full by ten in the morning. I understand the worry about theft, but a clear plastic bag or a quick bag check would solve the problem without leaving us stranded. Please reconsider. Lena Park, Class of 2028

What is the author’s main purpose in writing the letter?
options: To report a theft that occurred in the store
To explain how the lockers are assigned
To persuade the bookstore to change a rule
To thank the staff for a new service
items.explanation: The writer calls the rule unfair, offers alternatives such as clear bags or bag checks, and asks the store to reconsider, which is persuasion. The theft is mentioned only as the store’s concern, not reported as an event. The lockers are described as full, and the letter contains no thanks.

items.stem:
The bookstore’s new reading nook is, I say with some reluctance, wonderful. Two armchairs sit beside a window, and a shelf of staff favorites lists a reason for each pick in marker on index cards. I went in meaning to buy a pen and left forty minutes later with a novel I had never heard of. The checkout line was long, but nobody seemed bothered, and that is saying something at exam time.

Which phrase best describes the tone of the review?
options: resentful and bitter
admiring, with playful surprise
cautious and formal
indifferent and bored by the experience
items.explanation: The writer admits with some reluctance that the nook is wonderful, then jokes about going in for a pen and leaving with a novel, which gives an admiring and playful tone. There is no bitterness toward the store, the language is casual rather than formal, and a forty-minute visit shows interest instead of boredom.

items.stem:
Buyback schedule, Hartwell College bookstore. Buyback runs at the back counter on the last three days of exams, from nine until four. Books with a current edition are paid at half of the new price, while older editions are accepted only if the store has an order for them. Books with water damage or torn covers are refused. Students who cannot attend may leave books in the labeled bin near the entrance, and payment will be issued to their student accounts within a week.

According to the schedule, what happens to books left in the bin?
options: Payment is issued to the student’s account within a week
They are paid for at once in cash
They are refused because they were left unattended in the bin
They are donated to the bookstore
items.explanation: The schedule says students who cannot attend may use the bin and that payment goes to their student accounts within a week. Cash at the counter is not promised for bin drop-offs. Refusals apply only to damaged books, and nothing says that bin books become donations.

items.stem:
Shift notes, campus bookstore. During the first week of term, the line for course books wrapped around the corner of the building. By Thursday, Kofi had taped a laminated sign to the door listing the five most common courses and the aisle for each. Staff stopped answering the same question forty times a day, and the line moved faster. Kofi never mentioned the sign at the staff meeting; his manager found out when a customer thanked her.

What can be inferred about Kofi from the notes?
options: He dislikes helping customers
He made the sign because his manager ordered it
He solves problems without waiting for credit
He is unhappy with his job
items.explanation: Kofi made a helpful sign on his own and did not mention it at the meeting, so the manager learned of it from a customer, which suggests he works without seeking praise. The sign eased customers’ questions, so he does not dislike helping. It was his own idea, and nothing suggests dissatisfaction with the job.

items.stem:
The bookstore manager, Dr. Adaeze Lin, describes the spring rush as controlled chaos. Carts stand abandoned in the aisles, and students wave schedules over one another’s heads, yet the staff move through it with a calm that seems almost rehearsed. She says nobody panics, because everyone has been through worse in August. By closing time the shelves are straightened and the carts are back in their corner.

As used in the passage, what does the word “rehearsed” most nearly mean?
options: recently invented
badly performed by new staff
loudly announced
practiced in advance
items.explanation: The staff stay calm in the rush because they have been through worse in August, so their calm seems practiced in advance. The word does not mean recently invented, since the experience is long-standing. Nothing in the passage describes poor performance or an announcement made aloud.

items.stem:
A used textbook has several lives. It starts at the publisher’s warehouse and travels to the bookstore, where it is sold as new. After a semester, the student sells it back, and the store pays a portion of its price. The store then sorts it by edition, shipping outdated copies away and shelving current ones as used. The next student buys it at a lower price, completing the circle.

How is the passage mainly organized?
options: As a list of reasons why many students dislike used books
As a cycle that follows a book from first sale to resale
As a comparison of two publishers
As an argument against high textbook prices
items.explanation: The passage traces the book from warehouse to first sale, buyback, sorting and resale, and the closing phrase completing the circle signals a repeating cycle. It gives no reasons students dislike used books, compares no publishers, and does not argue about prices, though a lower resale price is mentioned.

items.stem:
Text 1: The study guide in the bookstore window is the best way to prepare for the chemistry final. Its practice problems match last year’s exam format, and the answer key explains each step.

Text 2: I bought the same guide and found it helpful but incomplete. The problems matched the exam format, yet the answer key skipped steps on the hardest ones, so I still needed office hours.

How do the two writers’ views of the guide differ?
options: Text 1 treats the answer key as thorough, but Text 2 finds it lacking
Text 1 questions the guide’s format, while Text 2 praises it
Text 2 says the problems are unrelated to the exam, and Text 1 disagrees
Both say the guide removes any need for office hours
items.explanation: Text 1 says the answer key explains each step, while Text 2 says it skipped steps on the hardest problems, which is the real difference. Both texts agree that the problems match the exam format. Text 2 admits needing office hours, so the guide did not remove that need.

items.stem:
Production schedule, Ridgeway Bread House. Bakers arrive at two in the morning to mix dough, which then rests for three hours so the flavor can develop. Loaves go into the oven at five and come out in staggered batches until seven. Pastries are assembled last because butter dough must stay cold, and they bake from seven to eight. The shop opens at eight, when the first customers usually begin lining up.

According to the schedule, why are pastries assembled last?
options: They bake longer than the loaves do
The shop opens before the loaves are done
Butter dough must stay cold
The bakers arrive too late to start them earlier
items.explanation: The schedule gives the reason directly: pastries are assembled last because butter dough must stay cold. Their baking window of seven to eight is no longer than the loaves’ window. The shop opens at eight, after all baking, and the bakers arrive at two in the morning, which is early, not late.

items.stem:
In August, Ridgeway Bread House started selling its day-old rolls at half price during the last hour before closing. The owner worried that customers would stop buying fresh rolls. Instead, waste fell because almost nothing was thrown away, and a group of evening regulars began to arrive just for the bargain. The owner later said the half-price hour was the cheapest advertising the shop had ever had.

What was the result of selling day-old rolls at half price?
options: Fresh rolls stopped selling well during the busy morning rush
Less food was thrown away, and new evening customers came
The bakery shortened its opening hours
The owner raised the price of fresh rolls
items.explanation: The passage says waste fell and evening regulars began to arrive for the bargain. The owner feared that fresh rolls would stop selling, but that did not happen. Nothing is said about shorter hours, and no price increase is mentioned anywhere in the passage, so the effect is on waste and evening sales.

items.stem:
Ridgeway Bread House says its sourdough stays fresh longer than supermarket bread. Its bakers point to the long, slow rise, which develops acids that slow mold. A customer survey in the shop found that most loaves bought on Saturday were still being eaten on Wednesday, while supermarket loaves usually went stale or were thrown out by Monday. The shop notes that its survey was small and informal.

Which detail best explains why the sourdough stays fresh longer?
options: Most Saturday loaves were still being eaten on Wednesday
Supermarket loaves were often thrown out by Monday
The shop’s survey was small and informal
The long, slow rise develops acids that slow mold
items.explanation: The acids produced during the slow rise are a reason for the freshness, which is what the question asks. The Wednesday result and the Monday comparison show the outcome, not the cause. The note that the survey was small and informal is a caution about the evidence, not an explanation.

items.stem:
My grandfather rose at three every morning to light the oven, and he treated the dough like a sleeping child. No slamming doors, no radio, no raised voices until the first loaf was out. I used to find the silence ridiculous. Now, standing alone in my own kitchen before dawn, I find myself whispering to the bowl. Some habits are not inherited so much as caught.

Which phrase best describes the tone of the passage?
options: scornful and dismissive
tense and fearful
fond and reflective
cheerful and boastful
items.explanation: The narrator once found the silence ridiculous but now whispers to the bowl, remembering the grandfather with affection and thinking about how habits pass on, which is fond and reflective. The narrator is no longer scornful, the mood is calm rather than fearful, and the closing thought is thoughtful, not boastful.

items.stem:
Ridgeway Bread House is hiring a weekend baker’s helper. The work begins at four in the morning and includes scaling ingredients, shaping rolls and washing equipment. Experience is not required, but applicants must be able to lift thirty pounds and arrive on time. Apply with a short note about why you want to work with bread, left at the front counter by Friday. Training is paid.

What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To teach readers how rolls are shaped
To describe the history of the bakery
To warn customers about weekend closings
To invite applicants to apply for a job
items.explanation: The notice lists duties, requirements, a deadline and paid training, so its purpose is to recruit applicants. Shaping rolls is named only as one duty, not taught. No bakery history is given, and there is no mention of weekend closings, only a weekend job that starts very early.

items.stem:
Text 1: A bakery should bake everything fresh each morning. Customers can taste the difference, and the smell of warm bread draws people through the door.

Text 2: Baking everything fresh sounds ideal, but small shops waste a great deal when they guess wrong about demand. Baking a smaller first batch and a second batch at noon keeps bread fresh and trims waste.

How does Text 2 respond to Text 1?
options: It accepts the goal of freshness but offers a way to avoid waste
It rejects freshness as unimportant to most of a bakery’s customers
It agrees that guessing demand is never a problem
It repeats the claim that the smell draws customers
items.explanation: Text 2 says fresh baking sounds ideal, so it accepts that goal, then proposes a smaller first batch and a noon batch to reduce waste. It never says customers do not care about freshness. It describes wrong guesses about demand as a real problem, and the smell of warm bread is raised only in Text 1.

items.stem:
After the fire station began visiting local schools, teachers sent home a card asking families to test their smoke alarms. Children returned signed slips saying the test had been done, and the station kept a tally of every slip. The station chief believes the program should expand to the middle school next year. She says that a child who has watched a firefighter explain an alarm will usually remind the whole household.

Which detail best supports the claim that the school visits led families to check their alarms?
options: The station began visiting local schools earlier in the same year
Children returned signed slips saying the test had been done
Teachers sent home a card with instructions
The chief believes the program should expand
items.explanation: Signed slips returned by children are direct evidence that families tested their alarms. The start of school visits and the cards sent home describe what the program did, not what resulted. The chief’s belief about expanding is an opinion about the future, not proof of what happened.

items.stem:
At the museum’s model railway, Wen is the self-appointed guardian of the miniature village. She straightens tiny fences, shoos curious fingers from the stations, and corrects visitors who call the trains toys. “These are scale models,” she says firmly, “and they are not for touching.” On busy Sundays she works from opening to closing without a break, and her vigilance has saved more than one tiny bridge.

As used in the passage, what does the word “vigilance” most nearly mean?
options: watchful attention
careless habit
friendly greeting
scheduled repair
items.explanation: Wen guards the village, shoos away fingers and works without a break, so her vigilance is watchful attention that protects the models. Carelessness is the opposite of what she shows. Her tone with visitors is firm rather than a friendly greeting, and a repair is something done after damage, not a type of watching.

items.stem:
Yeast is a living organism, a single-celled fungus that eats the sugars in flour. As it feeds, it releases carbon dioxide gas, which becomes trapped in the stretchy dough and makes it rise. Warmth speeds this process and cold slows it, which is why bakers can control a dough’s timing by choosing where to leave it. Too much heat, however, kills the yeast, and the dough will not rise at all.

What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Cold kills yeast faster than heat does
Yeast makes dough rise by releasing gas, and temperature matters
Flour already contains gas that bakers release by kneading it hard
Bakers prefer to keep dough as warm as possible
items.explanation: The passage explains that yeast feeds on sugars, releases gas that lifts the dough, and responds to warmth and cold. Cold only slows yeast, while too much heat kills it. The gas comes from the yeast, not from the flour or from kneading, and bakers choose a spot for the dough to control timing, not simply warmth.

items.stem:
Marlow Street Dance posted its fall class list on Monday. By Tuesday morning the beginner ballet class was full, and a handwritten note taped to the door said only, “Waitlist at the front desk, please be patient.” The desk clerk, Bruno, had started keeping a second list of names for a possible extra class. He told one parent he could not promise anything, but he asked for her phone number twice.

What can be inferred about Bruno from the passage?
options: He has already scheduled an extra class
He is annoyed by the long waitlist and the many questions
He thinks a second beginner class might be added
He wants parents to stop asking about classes
items.explanation: Bruno keeps a second list for a possible extra class and asks the parent for her number twice, which suggests he hopes a second class could be added, although he promises nothing. If he had scheduled it, he would not hedge. His effort to help parents shows he is not annoyed or trying to discourage them.
